description:
Find the best open-source handheld robot-gripper system for collecting manipulation demonstrations.

Replace the withdrawn ambidextrous-scissors idea. Jake wants people to hold and operate grippers directly while manipulating everyday objects, with geometry and observations that transfer well to the robot's end effector. The aim is scalable collection of useful action-aligned demonstrations: a practical medium-sized dataset, beyond a tiny teleoperation dataset, without relying on an enormous egocentric-video corpus. These are goals to evaluate, not proven sample-efficiency claims.

Start with existing context in plans/hand_1_0.md and plans/gripper_bet.md: the same camera-equipped gripper used handheld and on the SO-101. Related pebbles include voice-c7737295 (policy/model research), voice-40a92819 (LeHome), and voice-805d4970 (gripper design). Reconcile existing work rather than duplicating it. The spoken company reference may be Generalist Robotics; verify the intended reference and distinguish proprietary systems from genuinely open-source alternatives.

Research current primary sources, papers, repositories, hardware files, and licenses. Include UMI-style handheld demonstration systems and relevant newer alternatives. Compare hardware and software openness, build cost and availability, operator ergonomics, collection throughput, camera/pose/gripper-state synchronization, calibration and tracking failures, action representation, robot transfer and retargeting requirements, and compatibility with our SO-101 setup. Check what is actually released and reproducible rather than treating a demo video as a complete open-source system.

Evaluate published task success versus demonstration count and collection hours, dataset diversity, and training compute. Compare handheld gripper collection with conventional teleoperation and egocentric video where evidence supports a fair comparison. Clearly label missing evidence, incomparable benchmarks, and hypotheses; do not promise that one collection modality always needs less data.

Deliver a concise ranked shortlist with linked evidence, a best-fit recommendation for Helping Hands, and a small measurable pilot plan: parts/BOM, capture and training pipeline, representative manipulation tasks, data-quality checks, and success criteria before scaling collection. Explain whether to adopt an existing design or adapt Hand 1.0. Research and planning only; do not buy hardware or implement the design as part of this pebble.

results.identified_issue: Research via three web subagents (UMI family; Generalist AI + data-efficiency evidence; SO-101 fit). Many 2025-2026 sources were read through summarizing fetches; items marked (unverified) in plans/handheld_gripper.md were not confirmed from primary sources (Grabette license, HandUMI repo, part prices, SO-101 payload, SteamVR on macOS, ACT on MPS). Key reasoning: the robot knows its own EE pose via FK, so the tracker only rides on the handheld unit; what must match is camera + fingers (Hand 1.0 already enforces this). Handheld pipeline ends in SO-101 joint space (placo IK, feasibility/residual filter for the 5-DOF wrist) because FLUX 3 Action (plans/world_action_model.md) and ACT consume six joint channels — mirrors the only on-arm precedent robotfuel/so101_retargeted_umi (handheld ≈0.9× a teleop demo, n≤20). Rejected adopting UMI hardware (780 g, WSG-50 fingers, Max Lens Mod 1.0 discontinued, ORB-SLAM3 fragile), FastUMI/LEGATO (T265 EOL), AirExo-2 (NC license). Explicitly did not claim handheld needs fewer demos; the pilot's decisive criterion is equal human TIME, not equal demo count. Confirmed 'Generalist Robotics' = Generalist AI (GEN-0/1/1.5, wearable data, all proprietary) and updated gripper_bet.md's unverified note.
results.summary: Researched open handheld gripper systems and recommend adapting Hand 1.0 with an iPhone pose tracker, plus a small SO-101 pilot to prove it's worth it.
results.detailed_description:
The plan is in plans/handheld_gripper.md. The company is Generalist AI: their GEN-1 model is trained on data from cheap wearable devices on humans, and none of it is open. Of the open systems, UMI is still the best evidence, followed by Pollen's Grabette, the iPhone-tracked designs and UMI-3D. None of them is built for a 5-joint servo arm like the SO-101.

My recommendation is to adapt Hand 1.0 rather than adopt someone else's design. The robot already knows where its gripper is, so only the handheld unit needs a pose tracker. That can be an iPhone clipped onto the handheld unit only. Hand 1.0's trigger servo already records the grip in the robot's own units. Each handheld demo gets converted into the arm's joint angles, so it lands in the same dataset format as your teleop demos and FLUX.

The evidence doesn't show that handheld demos need fewer demos. The only test on an SO-101 found one handheld demo worth about 0.9 of a teleop demo. The case for handheld is that each demo is cheaper and faster to collect. So the pilot is a box pick-and-place, then paper, and it scores handheld against teleop at equal human time. New spend is under about $150 on top of Hand 1.0.

Three calls for you, listed at the end of the doc: iPhone as the tracker, running the pilot after the first FLUX test, and Hand 1.0's open decisions.
